Mr. MacNICOL; Referring to the item for the new supreme court building, I wish to say a word in reference to the heating and air conditioning. I have no doubt that the design of the building generally is very beautiful; from what we can see so far it

looks as if it is going to be a splendid addition to the public buildings of Ottawa. But looking over the specifications for the 'heating I find that notwithstanding that the hot water main which heats all these central buildings runs right under it, the new supreme court building is to be heated by another system. The engineer who laid out the first central heating plant for the government buildings was one of the eminent engineers of America, Mr. Melvern F. Thomas. He worked under two celebrated architects. He laid out what was designed to be the most economical heating system possible, which I believe it is. It is so efficient that this whole central building is heated for four months during the winter, without a dollar of cost, from exhaust steam which operates some of the equipment in the central boiler plant along the river, and which would otherwise go to waste. I do not know whether the engineers of the department have approved this proposed heating system; I intend to find out. I know from long experience that the department has a heating engineer of very high standing, whose name, I understand, is-
Mr. F. O. Hamel.

I was thinking of
Mr. Hamel, who is one of the most competent and efficient engineers in Canada. I have the utmost confidence in Mr. Hamel, and if he has approved what is going in there, I would have nothing more to say on the subject.
In years past I had a good deal to do with this type of engineering, although perhaps I have now forgotten most of what I knew. But I know well the cardinal objectives we kept before us in laying out -hot-water heating and air-conditioning systems, the latter having come in about the time I left that calling. As objective number one we kept before us the most satisfactory equipment. Number two was to keep down the first cost, so far as might be consistent with first-class equipment. The third objective was low cost of maintenance, and the fourth was low cost, of operation. The original system specified for the central heating of all these government buildings fulfilled all four of these cardinal objectives. In our central heating plant in Ottawa I believe we have one of the most economical systems, if not the most economical in Canada. It is what is known as a forced hot water system. The specifications for the mechanical apparatus for the supreme court building which I have here call for a large amount of the most complicated equipment, to which I shall refer in a moment. I am satisfied that had they called for the same type of system as that by

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
which this building is heated it might not cost half as much money. I may be wrong, but the departmental engineers can tell; I know the minister has altogether too much to do to deal with a matter of this kind, and perhaps he does not bother with it at all. I am going to ask the minister to ask his chief engineer whether the system which is to foe installed in the supreme court building, if it is anything like what I have just said, will not be much more costly than would have been the *case if that building had been heated by forced hot water from the central heating plant.
Then there is the cost of maintenance. From my own experience I am as sure as I can be that the cost of maintaining this proposed heating system will be infinitely greater than the cost of maintaining a system such as we have in this building. To begin with I believe there are six pumps to take the condensation back to the central boiler building. So far as I know there are only two pumps used for forcing hot water through the whole central block of buildings. How many judges have we down there at the supreme court, or how many are we going to have? Are there to be a hundred or two hundred judges, to require such an extensive heating system and so much equipment?
Then I am sure the cost of operation, with these batteries of pumps, motors and valves to reduce the high pressure steam to low pressure-which would be wholly unnecessary if the central heating plant had been used- will be much greater. I am not finding fault with the plan; this proposed system may be so perfect that there has never been anything like it in the world before, and that may account for the costly equipment that is called for. As I understand it, the central heating plant which serves this central block of buildings requires only a few operators, but I believe it will take quite a staff to operate all the equipment to be installed in this new building. Nothing can be done about it now, because I believe all the contracts have been let, but I hope in future whoever is Minister of Public Works will see to it that the chief engineer of the department-one of the best in Canada-gives his O.K. to whatever equipment is used in government buildings erected in this central group in this city. I do not say that O.K. has not been given in this case, but I should like to know whether or not it has. I have a very high regard for the chief engineer, and I can hardly conceive that he would O.K. what is going in the supreme court building.
Then, when it comes to air-conditioning, one night on my way to Toronto I overheard
a conversation between two engineers. I did not know them then. I do not know them now, but having had some experience in air conditioning a few years ago I at once pricked up my ears and became interested in what they were saying. What they said may not be true, but they were very hostile about the fact that they could not figure on the air conditioning equipment. One of them said, "There is no equipment like it in Canada, and I know of only one similar installation in the United States." He may not have known of all the equipment of that type that has been installed in the United States; there may be installations for all he knew and for all I know.	What I paid particular
attention to, however, was their attitude towards a situation to which I have always been very hostile myself; that is, a specification sewed up so tight that only one firm could figure on it. I can remember back some years to when I used to call on the engineers of the Department of Public Works in this city to discuss specifications. Never did I suggest to them to specify one line of equipment. I always suggested to leave their specifications open, merely calling for standard Canadian material and one hundred per cent efficiency. I heard one engineer tell the other, "I saw so and so, and it was no use; I could not figure on it." The other gentleman replied that he could not figure on it either; then I became interested and looked into the matter.
I have in my hand one of the principal engineering journals of the United States, which is called Heating, Piping and AirConditioning, which gives the names of many of the leading firms manufacturing air conditioning equipment, such as:	Baker Ice
Machine, Worthington, Air Temp, Curtis, Brunner, York-perhaps the oldest of all and the one with the most experience, according to this magazine, having been manufacturing for fifty-four years-Carrier, which I believe is installed in the new Bank of Canada building, Kelvinator, Frick, Vilter and many others. Each of these famous companies has been barred from figuring on this equipment. I have been told, and I believe the statement to be correct-though of course I speak subject to correction-that according to these specifications only one firm, whose name I do not know, could figure on this installation. I heard one of the engineers add, "And it costs twice as much." Similar equipment might have been supplied for half the price, but it may be that the type that is being installed is worth twice as much; I do not know, but I do maintain that these specifications should

Supply-Public W orks-Buildings
have been wide open so that any company manufacturing one hundred per cent efficient equipment could have had the opportunity of figuring.
I want to be fair; I am not finding fault with what is going in, because for all I know this may be the finest equipment made. What I am finding fault with is that any specifications of the dominion government should be so sewed up that only one firm [DOT] could figure. And I do stress the fact that of all the buildings in this central heating area the one above all others that should have been heated from the central heating plant is the new supreme court building. Why, the forced hot-water main runs right underneath the supreme court building, but these specifications call for a main bringing steam into the new building, which steam will have to be greatly reduced in pressure before it can be used.
Then I find that the specifications call for 500 gallons of hot water per hour, or two batteries of 250 gallons each, to provide the hot water for domestic purposes. Well, the judges must be going to wash themselves every second and a half. They will be able to invite all the judges in Canada to come there and wash, and still there will be lots of hot water. We have nothing like that in this main building. The equipment in use here is modern ; I venture to say that it costs little to operate or maintain, and certainly it is very satisfactory. You cannot turn on a hot water faucet anywhere in this building where you will not find plenty of hot water available.
I do not want the minister to think I am finding fault, 'because I am not. Having had experience in this line of business, however, and having accidentally overheard the conversation to which I referred, I thought it my duty to inquire into the matter and this is the result of my inquiries.

I must thank my hon. friend for the moderation of his observations on a question about which hd seems to be much concerned and, so far as I can gather from his remarks, in connection with which he has had some experience. I am told that the new supreme court building is to be heated from the central heating plant in Ottawa. There may have been some discussion between the architect who designed the building, the assistant architect, and the assistant engineer in the department who looks after heating, as to what systems and methods of procedure should be used, but my information is that all points have been cleared up and an agreement has been concluded so far as heating is concerned. My information also is that there will be no large increase

in the staff in order to take care of the system and that it will not cost any more than any ordinary system. Of course, I speak subject to correction because I have not the details before me, and I am sure my hon. friend would not expect me to have all this information. The department is open to my hon. friend, and I invite him to come and discuss this matter with the engineers. He will be welcome and we will take advantage of his experience.
There was also a certain amount of discussion between the officers of the department and the architect in connection with the air-conditioning system. After discussing various points they came to an understanding as to the system to be used. The specifications were not drawn with a view to favouring any firm or individual. We always take care in the department not to bind ourselves to any class of material or to any firm or manufacturer. We try to leave matters open to all contractors and manufacturers provided they can produce the results we expect from the machinery or supplies required. The machinery and materials going to make up the air-conditioning system which will be installed in the supreme court building will be supplied by Canadian firms.

And manufactured in
Canada?
Manufactured in Canada.
One hundred per cent?

One hundred per cent.
Perhaps I am answering a little too quickly, but I would say that the percentage of Canadian labour in the system we are installing is much greater than it would be in any other system proposed. My hon. friend has referred to certain firms, but if my information is correct they are all United States firms which do not manufacture in Canada to any extent. It .may be a compliment to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard), but the firm manufacturing this system is located in that city. I repeat what I said in connection with the heating system. The air-conditioning system will not be installed for some time, and I invite my hon. friend to give us the benefit of his views and experience in connection with matters of this kind. I can assure him that we are not paying any substantially greater amounts for the heating and air-conditioning systems we are installing in the supreme court building. If my hon. friend is able to convince me to the contrary after discussing the matter with the officers of my department, I am open to conviction.

Supply-Public Works-Buildings

In view of the fact that the hot-water main which heats this building runs right under the new supreme court building I cannot understand why an engineer would specify anything but hot-water heating for that building. However, I shall be glad to accept the minister's invitation to investigate further. I did not want to do that before bringing up the matter in the committee. The engineers that I overheard on the train must have been entirely mistaken because one said to the other that the air-conditioning system was not being manufactured in Canada. I do not know what type of equipment is being used in the Bank of Canada building, but it seems to be giving first-class satisfaction. I am glad to hear that the equipment which has been OJCd by the minister is to be made in the home town of my genial, good natured and good looking friend, the hon. member for Sherbrooke.

With a view to stimulating employment in Canada and in an effort to relieve the unemployment situation, between the years 1930 and 1933, I think somewhere around 1932, the Department of Public Works introduced a standard clause into all specifications in connection with contracts let by that department. This clause provided that the materials required in the construction or operation of a building must be, first, Canadian if available; second, British if available, and then if they could not be obtained from Canadian or British sources, resort could be had to other sources of supply. From what the minister 'has said, I assume that this standard clause is still in the specifications of the Department of Public WTorks. I am glad to hear that, and I hope it will continue to be used. I think Canadian manufacturers can supply practically every kind of material and equipment satisfactory for Canadian requirements.
This item for the supreme court building is $1,300,000. Frankly, that appears to be a large expenditure for a building to provide accommodation for nine judges-seven supreme court judges and two exchequer court judges. There will be judges' chambers and library accommodation, which will probably be extensive. The supreme court has the finest legal library in Canada, and the present accommodation is altogether inadequate. I have no doubt that suitable and ample accommodation is being provided for the protection and expansion of that excellent library. Then there is the courtroom itself, which by the way does not require to accommodate a vast number of people. Not many people" attend the sittings of the court in the ordinary course apart from counsel and
those immediately interested in the sittings. The building itself is large in extent and, of course, must be modern in every respect, but $1,300,000 does appear a large amount. What is the reason for this cost? I admit that a building which houses the Supreme Court of Canada ought to be beautiful, and fine from an architectural point of view; it should be good in every sense of the word.
Someone has stated, and I believe it is correct, that extensive garage accommodation is being provided in connection with the building. Accommodation of that kind is perhaps necessary and desirable, and that may in some measure account for what looks like a large expenditure. If the minister could justify what does appear to be a very large expenditure on a comparatively small building, I am sure the committee would be pleased to receive his explanation.

First, I must say that the terraces surrounding the building and the garage accommodation are included in the cost. So far as the general requirements for the building are concerned, the architect, before ever he started on his designs for the building, had several consultations with the chief justice of the supreme court and with the judges of the exchequer court, which is also to be housed in this building and after checking up on the recommendations and requests made by the judges of the supreme court, and particularly the chief justice, the architect began work on his designs. He did not start by designing and then afterwards ask the judges if they were satisfied; he consulted them first, and the building he has designed answers the requirements placed before him and before a committee by the judges of the supreme court. I think that is the proper way for an architect to proceed in designing a building of any kind, to make sure first what the requirements as to floor space are, and then make his designs in accordance with the requirements. That is the general procedure followed, and I am informed that the building as it has been designed by the architect meets the requirements of the judges of the supreme court.
I confess to my hon. friend that I am not competent to go into all the details, but I heartily endorse what he has said as to the importance of having a building of which we shall be proud rather than ashamed for the housing of the highest tribunal in this land, and possibly our court of last resort if a proposal now before the house is carried out. I think it is a good investment for a country like Canada to have, as my hon. friend suggests, a building which will be a source of pride to house the highest tribunal of the

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
dominion. There is no extravagance about the building. It is simply being built in accordance with the requirements and the desire to have a building in which we can take pride and which visitors to our country will look upon with a certain degree of satisfaction.

In a general way I agree entirely with what the minister states as to the nature of the building. Would he tell the committee the extent of the garage accommodation that is being provided, how many cars will be accommodated, who will make use of the garage space provided, and also give the name of the contractor?

The contractor is the
Anglin-Norcross Corporation, which is a reputable firm. The garage space will accommodate 165 cars. It is to be used not only by people in the supreme court building but by people working in the neighbouring buildings.
Will they pay rent for the use of the garage for their cars?
So far no provision has been made as to rental. That may be considered.
I do not see why they should be rent free when all the rest of us have to pay rent.
What is the estimated cost of completing this building?
The total cost, when everything is completed, will be a little over three million dollars.

A return that was brought down for me a short time ago gave the estimated cost to complete as $3,360,000. We know that the justice building, which is completed, cost $1,365,811.37, and it is a great deal larger than the supreme court building. What is the reason for the big difference in the cost. I was in a committee not long ago where one hon. gentleman opposite made the statement that we were erecting a building costing $5,000,000 to house five men. I do not agree with him. We are putting up a building which will cost $3,360,000 to house seven men. I should like to know the reason for the difference in the cost between the justice building and the supreme court building.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The
supreme court building is to house the litigants of Canada who come to the supreme court. It is not seven men; it is the whole of Canada.

I wish to take issue with the minister. To house the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the justice department we
(Mr. Cardin.)
had a building erected at a cost of $1,365,000, while the supreme court building is to cost pretty nearly double, $3,360,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not the same type of building.
But consider what we are housing in each instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no court house in the mounted police building.

The estimated cost for the building itself is $2,500,000. The balance goes for supervision, fittings, the library, equipment for the whole building, provision for a garage and the terraces surrounding the building.
What is the total cost?
The estimated total cost is $3,360,000, which includes the building itself, the equipment of the interior, the terraces surrounding the building, and the garage.
But take the justice building; surely the sum of $1,365,811.37 includes the fittings as well. We have not any garage there. That includes everything?

I am informed1 that the
figure my hon. friend has mentioned does not include interior fittings of the justice building. That is only for the building.
That is the total cost as supplied to me by the department.
Well, for the building itself, probably. But it is not the same class of building.
It is on the same return.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I
say a word about that? The justice building is an office building. Surely my hon. friend does not think that the Supreme Court of Canada should have an office building? There are three powers in this land: the legislative power, the executive power, and the judicial power. My hon. friend is a part of the legislative power; he is well housed in this building, which has cost a good deal more than the supreme court building will cost. The executive power is housed in all the buildings of the government of Canada. It was a disgrace to this country to have the supreme court, the highest court of the land, housed in this old workshop. I remember that when the attorney general of Australia was here a few years ago and I was the Minister of Justice, he wanted to go to the supreme court and I was ashamed to take him to that building. It is high time that we in Canada

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
should have a supreme court building which is in harmony with the buildings of the other powers of the land, and one of which every Canadian may be proud.

I certainly agree with the
Minister of Justice that the housing of the supreme court has been a disgrace. But the question I have raised about the cost was stated by one of his own supporters in the committee. The difference in the cost of the two buildings is one which concerns the public of this country.

My opinion is that there
are no departments so antiquated as the public works department and the Post Office Department. They seem to have no business administration whatever; nobody seems to know anything about what anything costs or what it may cost. I have no more complaint to make of the present Minister of Public Works than of any of his predecessors. All of them appear to be imbued with the same spirit; they do not seem to know anything nor do they want to know anything. If they had a proper accounting system, as they should have, when the Post Office Department or any other department asked for a building of certain dimensions the public works department should be able to say, "That will cost you so much." Nothing is charged against the Post Office Department, and that department reports that it makes a million and a half dollars a year. It is charged nothing by the public works department for providing the cleaning, the extra men and the other services pertaining to the post office. I have repeatedly suggested to the committee that the public works department should charge against each department what it does for that department and so ascertain what that department is costing.
The hon. member for Davenport gave a good illustration of how things are operating at present. The system which heats this building goes under the justice building, yet a new heating system is supplied for that building alone. All the administration buildings should be under the same system, which could then be operated at half the cost that is required to-day. There is no study of economy. I find the same trouble with all the Postmasters General; they do not seem to know anything; they do not care to know anything; but I will say this, that the last Postmaster General was getting nearer to perfection than any other Postmaster General I ever knew. The first year he came here he knew nothing at all; the next year he improved. The third year he improved yet further and was able to give us a certain
amount of information. Now we have another Postmaster General starting in new, and I suppose he will not know much until he has been here for some years. I am not criticizing particularly the individual, but I say that the whole administration of this government is absolutely rotten to the core from the point of view of economy. I do not mean that there is any graft; I say that no consideration at all is given to administration from the point of view of economy.
What about the former government?

The hon. member did not hear me eulogizing the former government, did he? Governments of all kinds are the same. But when the leader of the last government was in power, one could not get away with much extravagance, because he was keeping his eye on everything. He had an eye to business, and nobody could get away with anything which was not entirely legal, honourable and honest. In so far as spending money was concerned, I will say that for the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, the former leader of our party.
He has taken his eye off you now.

I cannot hear the hon. member. It is a shame that when the public works department do a job for any other department, it is not charged up to the department which receives the service. If that were done we could find out how much the Post Office Department makes. As I stated before, they tell you they make so many millions a year, but so many items are not charged against them that at the end of the year they do not know whether they make or lose. That is no way for any department to be run, and that kind of thing goes on because the public works department has no proper accounting system and does not know what it is doing. It is not a good method of administration; the whole thing should be changed so that we may know exactly what each department is losing or making. At any rate that is my view of the matter from a business point of view. There is not a bit of excuse for the Minister of Public Works, because he is just as smooth as anybody else and he can rise in his place and make excuses all the time for what he is doing; but when he tells you that if the post office makes a demand for a building he must consent to it, he knows quite well that he can refuse to construct a building which is larger than is required, or he can tell the department, "You do not need a building at all." That is what he
4832	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Buildings
should be prepared to say if necessary, and if he has not that power he should not be public works minister at all. I hope the government will show some common sense and try to administer the affairs of the nation as a private firm administers its own business. We can all realize that any company which ran its business in the way that this government administers the business of this country would go bankrupt in no time, because its present methods are nothing but a waste of money in order to please this, that or the other fellow who wants a contract or something of the kind.
I hate to repeat what I have said; but as the hon. member for Davenport pointed out, this heating system is just one indication of the lack of decent, good judgment. In the city of Toronto all these buildings are centrally heated; The Royal York and station "A" are heated by the one system, the same as are the parliament buildings and the colleges. Why could not all the buildings- the administrative blocks, the justice building and the new supreme court building-be heated by the same system so that a great deal of money would be saved? Economy everywhere should be our watchword. We must do everything we can to save money in the interests of Canada and of the common people. Our debts are growing; our taxpayers are getting harder up, and the time is coming when the whole thing will stop, because this country's obligations cannot be carried much longer by only eleven million people. They are all bankrupt even though they will not admit it.

Will the hon. member
answer a question?

If the hon. member will
speak up, I will answer it if I can.

Is the hon. member figuring that the Department of Public Works should be a money-making proposition, or is the purpose of the department to try to develop and assist Canada in different directions-to do something for the nation?

I would not say that it
was a money-making proposition. The trouble is simply carelessness and indifference as to how money is being spent, and probably trying to oblige a number of political friends to whom they want to give a contract or something of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You are
pretty bad!

Perhaps my first word
should be, on behalf of ministers of the department, of the past, of the present and of the

future, one of grateful acknowledgement to the tribute which the hon. member who has just spoken has paid us.
Which member?

We will take the compliments from whatever source they come; they are rare indeed. The other item in regard to which I should like to get some additional information is the one of $295,000 which reads:
Ottawa, improvements to confederation park, including compensation to Ottawa Electric Railway Company.
We know that some quite impressive, extensive and beautiful improvements have been made recently in the city of Ottawa round confederation park. A wonderful improvement has taken place. But here we have $295,000 which this government is contributing, and in it is included an item of compensation to the Ottawa Electric Railway Company. I understand that some of the tracks of that company in this area were taken up and their use for street-cars was, of course, discontinued. Buses have been substituted. How much was paid to the company in this connection?
It occurs to me that the present tendency is to get away from street-cars and to use buses instead. In fact, I doubt very much whether any company starting in the field of providing transportation in a city like Ottawa would put down tracks at all. There are disadvantages and objections to their use. There is no elasticity to the service provided by the old fixed and established trolley and track system. The new system of buses involves a smaller initial capital investment, provides greater elasticity of service and enables the company from time to time to adapt their service to changing conditions and developments, to movements from one part of the city to another even from day to day, and on special occasions to accommodate that service to the volume of traffic that is moving in the city as a whole or in any particular area. What does suggest itself to one is that under such conditions it would be really to the advantage of the Ottawa Electric Railway Company to adopt a bus service, and the wonder is why they should get some compensation for adapting their service to modern requirements. Perhaps the minister would break down the item and give us the expenditures in different directions, indicating particularly how much is involved in this particular item to which I refer.

This amount of $295,000 is to provide for the completion of all improvements to confederation park, including the

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
widening of the bridge, construction of roadways and sidewalks, terracing round the national memorial, and so forth. I can give the various details if the hon. member would like to have them.
Please.

These are the amounts:
Improvements to confederation park and widening bridge, under contract, Goldie Construction Company, $10,000.
Roadways, sidewalks, terracing around national memorial, under contract with Robertson company, $178,000.
Re federal district commission, grading roads, etc., $20,000.
Sidewalks and roadways, $27,000.
Compensation to Ottawa street railway, $25,000.
Supervision, $2,744.
Contingencies, $31,000.
We are paying this compensation to the Ottawa Electric Railway Company to induce them to make a real start in the abolition of the street railways and the adoption of the bus system. Perhaps as a general rule it might cost the company in the long run less to operate buses than to continue with the use of car tracks, but that is not true when they are starting on the movement. They have to be to some extent induced to abandon the old system and adopt the new. Had we not contributed this sum of $25,000 to the company we should have been forced to pay a certain amount for re-laying the tracks along Elgin street joining the island in confederation park. That amount would have been more than $12,000. We would have had to pay them that sum, and the old system would still have remained. We thought it advisable therefore, with a view to getting a start in the right direction, to make the contribution. Moreover, it adds to the beauty of the park. The street railway company absolutely refused to agree to the change without compensation. They believed that they could continue to their own advantage the use of car tracks on Elgin street for a number of years without having to think of changing to the new system. The existing equipment would have lasted a long while, and it would have been to their advantage not to undertake any new capital expenditure in procuring buses. It was with a view to facilitating and hastening the change as far as possible that we agreed to the compensation, so that the buses could be introduced this year instead of next year or two or three years hence. This amount is partly compensated by the amount we saved, which would otherwise have been paid for re-laying the tracks on Elgin street.
Just a word on this excellent development. I fancy that if the whole cost were tabulated it would run into many millions. We removed the old Russell hotel and theatre and the church-
And the post office.
And the post office, and the total cost would amount to over five million dollars.
Away more than that.

Well, many millions of dollars. I notice already that the dear people of Ottawa are acquiring the habit of parking cars, some not bad looking cars, many of them disreputable looking, round the islands in the square. Surely we have not spent many millions of dollars to provide a cheap parking place for residents of Ottawa.
That will not be tolerated.
But it is being tolerated, and once a thing like that starts-I notice it every evening-
They may be the cars of persons working there.
No, they are not, because they come there and stay for several hours when the men are not working at all.
The situation will be changed when the work is completed.

I spoke to some of the police in an informal way, and they said they were having and would have great difficulty in dealing with the matter. When a thing like that starts, it is extremely difficult to stop it. Cars should not be allowed to park there, because it destroys the beauty of the whole area. Millions of dollars having been expended for beautifying that area-and it is a magnificent job, apart from the cost feature-let us see to it that the Ottawa folk do not get started using it as a cheap parking place, ,
What is the cost of this work? Does confederation park include Connaught place? What is the expenditure to date, including the memorial?

The expenditure for that park is nearly two million dollars. That includes the monument itself, which cost $168,223. The contract awarded to Cape and Company for the granite work of the monument totalled $124,573. The contract to A. W. Robertson and Company for the steps and sidewalks and renovation of the streets

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
and terraces amounted to $191,000-I am leaving out the odd figures. The contract to Goldie Construction Company for the widening of the bridge over the canal and the tracks was $325,912. Then there is compensation to Ottawa electric railway, $25,000, and incidentals including work done by federal district commission, $50,000. And I am including the construction of the new post office at the corner of Sparks and Elgin streets, the cost of which is going to be $644,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not part of the park.
For that building, $644,000?
Yes. And the properties that we expropriated at the comer of Sparks and Elgin streets cost $396,000.
What is that for?

That is the expropriation of the two Hope properties and one Booth property, the site of the new post office. The total of the items I have just given is $1,924,000. That, I take it, would be the cost of confederation park as we have it now.
What about the expropriation of the Russell hotel and the church?

I was just going to mention that this does not include the cost of expropriation of the old Russell hotel and the old buildings. This takes into account the development of the park as we started to make it in the last two years.
What is the cost of the other expropriation?
Unfortunately I have not that now.
It runs into several million dollars.
Oh, yes.
Another item is the Peterborough public building, estimated cost $250,000. I suppose that building will provide for all the public services there?
Yes.
As I recall it, we already have a public building there now?
Yes.
What is to be done with the old building? Is it to be abandoned entirely?

We have not yet decided what we will do with that building, but representations were made to me that the

service could not be properly accommodated in the buildings we have in Peterborough; that a new building was required to meet the needs of the service in that city.

It is not a new issue; the question of a public building for Peterborough has been up for some years. Apparently they have been able to make out a better case in the last year or two than they were able to put forward in years gone by. As I recall it, the case was not a convincing one. Perhaps they have been able to bring some additional, more powerful arguments, to bear upon the minister than those they were able to bring in years gone by when conditions were practically the same.
There is in this vote another item upon which I think the minister should make a complete, comprehensive and chronological statement to the committee in considerable detail; that is, the public building at Tweed. The minister knows quite well that this has been the subject of extensive and sustained newspaper comment in Ontario. It is one of those cases that crop up from time to time where there is a dispute in the community, first as to the site of a public building, and a real difference of opinion as to whether a public building is necessary at all. As I recall it, the policy of the department in years gone by when these disputes arose was to wait and allow the local parties to compose their differences before a public building was constructed. That seems to me a sound policy. So long as a community is divided in opinion as to the site of a public building or the need for it the public vrorks department should go slowly about taking any action whatever until the municipality is agreed as to the site or the need for the building. If I am correctly informed, that situation has not been reached, in Tweed. One site was acquired; it was sold and negotiations took place between the municipality and the government in connection with an exchange of site. Finally another site was selected in a different part of the town, again against the wish of the municipal council, and against resolutions and petitions sent in by the residents of that municipality.
If I am correct in that statement, which is the one that has appeared in the press, I am at a loss to understand why there should be such persistence on the part of the Department of Public Works in forcing a public building upon this community. I believe this is a case in which the minister should be prepared to make a complete statement, because if the condition is as I have stated, it is a very disturbing state of affairs, which is altogether unsatisfactory and certainly should be cleared up. So I ask the minister to give

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
the committee, in his own way and from the beginning, a complete, chronological, comprehensive review of the whole situation, including the decision finally arrived at and the reasons for that decision, whether or not this building is to be constructed and any other information the minister feels should be given to the public at this time in explanation of this extraordinary situation.

Certainly I would have
felt a great deal more uneasy than I do at the moment if the discussion of this item had occurred a month ago, because in the interval new developments have taken place which entirely change the picture that has been drawn by my hon. friend. The construction of this building was decided a couple of years ago, and a site was acquired in what is known as the southern section of the village of Tweed. Representations were made to the department that this site was not proper and that it would not be convenient for the population to have a public building erected at that location. As a result of these representations the department did not proceed with the building but looked round for another site, which we discovered in the northern section of the village and acquired in exchange for the first site. We advertised for tenders, and when we were nearly at the point of awarding the contract, representations were made by members of the municipal council and others to the effect that the second site was not satisfactory to the residents of the village. I received petitions, letters and delegations supporting both sides of the argument. Some desired to have the public building on the site in the northern part of the village, commonly known as the Quinn site. Others said that site was no good because it was not in the centre of the community. Resolutions were passed by the municipal council protesting against the construction of that building on the Quinn site, and I continued to receive petitions and delegations suggesting that we should seek still another site.

This again is rather a long item. The first that attracts attention is drainage schemes, $100,000. Would the minister give some details of that? Are there any new ones? I know there are some old ones that were hanging round. I know it is hardly consistent with the policy of the department to take on too many new ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I remember my hon. friend originated some of them.

No, we tried to finish some that I think my hon. friend originated, and we were not very successful in terminating them. The difficulty about these is they are really interminable. Once you begin them you find many creeks running into the original drainage scheme.

In large measure I agree with the comment of my hon. friend that the moment you commence a drainage proposal it is very hard to stop it. This item was included to meet a number of requests coming to the department from Ontario and Quebec for small projects; it does not cover any large
4844	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Harbours and Rivers
project at all. The idea is to meet the requirements of the residents of poor municipalities and parishes who cannot obtain assistance from the provincial governments. They come to us asking for the expenditure of a little money in these small, usually isolated localities not only to help improve the lands upon which, generally speaking, newcomers are being established, but also to expend a certain amount of money in these localities in order to help these people keep body and soul together. This expenditure relates perhaps more particularly to sections where colonization is being carried on. My hon. friend can take my word for it that I have no idea of going into any large scheme in regard to these drainage proposals. My contention is that they are provincial rather than federal undertakings.
Absolutely.

But we have done so many of these little works already, practically all over the country, that at this time, while there is a certain amount of distress, I did not think we should refuse to carry on and help, in that limited way, a number of small, poor communities in Ontario and Quebec.
My hon. friend has referred to works carried on in the past along this line. I must confess that the federal government has spent a large amount of money to assist in draining land in Quebec and Ontario, and I assume, to a certain extent in other provinces; and although we do not admit or recognize any real responsibility under the cold letter of the law, I imagine it is only fair that we should show a little goodwill towards these poor parishes and municipalities by helping improve their land, at the same time spending a few dollars to help relieve the limited unemployment that exists even in these localities. We speak of trying to keep people on the land. Well, while properly speaking this does not come within our jurisdiction, I think it only fair that we do something to encourage these people to stay on the land instead of coming to the towns and cities, where they become a much greater burden to the public.

Does the province, the
municipality or the parish contribute to the cost of these works?

Not exactly. There is no
understanding, but legislation has been enacted in the province of Quebec dealing with the improvement of the drainage of lands generally, and from the correspondence I have already received I understand they look to the provincial government to contribute a certain amount of money under that legislation to meet the drainage requirements in connec-

tion with these lands. It is a new thing, I admit, but after all it is a small matter. I propose to check it, and if I am not here probably my hon. friend will continue the policy of checking these expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He entertains no such hope.

The minister has furnished much better arguments than I could advance as to why an item of this kind should not appear in the estimates. This concerns a purely provincial matter. I think this error began in connection with some drainage scheme in the vicinity of Beauharnois. The amount of this vote, a round sum of S100,000, suggests that possibly the minister has no particular schemes in mind, but that he is providing this $100,000 for safety purposes, in case he should become convinced that any of these schemes are worthy or should be undertaken. I notice he has not given the details of any scheme.
I have none.

Then it is just a sort
of accident insurance the minister is taking out, possibly also against political accidents.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. There is one large amount concerning the Richelieu river which will require some discussion and as to which some information will be asked. It is now eleven o'clock, and I would suggest that the committee rise. The minister has made pretty good progress.
Progress reported.
